lesson.title: Strength in Numbers: How Solute Particles Change a Solvent's Behavior
lesson.summary: Colligative properties are changes in a solvent's physical behavior that depend only on how many solute particles are dissolved in it, not on what those particles are.
lesson.body:
When you dissolve something in a liquid, the liquid itself starts to behave differently: it boils at a higher temperature, freezes at a lower one, and exerts less vapor pressure than it did when pure. What is striking about these changes is that they do not depend on whether the dissolved substance is salt, sugar, or antifreeze; they depend only on how many particles are floating around in the solution. Properties with that peculiar feature are called colligative properties, from a Latin root meaning "bound together," because they are governed collectively by particle count rather than particle identity. The four classic examples are vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and osmotic pressure. The next two chapters go deep on boiling point elevation and freezing point depression; this chapter builds the shared foundation underneath all four.

That foundation rests on two ideas you have already met: Solutions and Mole Fraction. A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent, and the mole fraction X of any component is its moles divided by the total moles of everything present. Mole fraction matters here because Raoult's law, which describes vapor pressure lowering, is written directly in terms of it: the vapor pressure of a solution equals the mole fraction of the solvent times the vapor pressure of the pure solvent, or P_solution = X_solvent times P-degree. Notice that adding solute particles necessarily shrinks X_solvent below 1, which is precisely why the vapor pressure drops. The more solute particles you add relative to solvent, the more the vapor pressure falls, regardless of what the solute is chemically.

The phrase "regardless of what the solute is" needs one important qualification: it is the number of particles that counts, not the number of formula units you weighed out. A mole of glucose dissolves as one mole of individual glucose molecules, so it contributes one mole of particles. A mole of sodium chloride, however, is an ionic compound that dissociates completely in water into one mole of Na+ ions and one mole of Cl- ions, for a total of two moles of particles. Chemists track this with the van't Hoff factor, i, defined as the number of particles a formula unit produces in solution. For glucose and other molecular nonelectrolytes, i = 1. For NaCl, i = 2. For a compound like CaCl2, which dissociates into one Ca2+ and two Cl-, i = 3. Every colligative property equation you will use includes this factor, because a mole of NaCl genuinely disrupts the solvent about twice as much as a mole of glucose does.

Consider a worked example of vapor pressure lowering using Raoult's law. Suppose you dissolve 1.00 mol of glucose, a nonelectrolyte with i = 1, into 9.00 mol of water, and the pure water in this system has a vapor pressure of approximately 23.8 torr. The total moles of particles in solution are 9.00 mol water plus 1.00 mol glucose particles, giving 10.00 mol total, so the mole fraction of water is X_water = 9.00 / 10.00 = 0.900. Applying Raoult's law, P_solution = 0.900 times 23.8 torr = 21.42 torr. The vapor pressure lowering is the difference: 23.8 minus 21.42 equals 2.38 torr. You can verify the multiplication directly: 23.8 times 9 equals 214.2, and dividing by 10 gives 21.42, confirming the result.

The reason all of this matters beyond vapor pressure is that boiling point elevation and freezing point depression are really just downstream consequences of this same vapor pressure change. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the surrounding atmospheric pressure, so if dissolving a solute lowers the vapor pressure, the solution has to be heated further before it reaches that threshold, raising the boiling point. Freezing is the reverse story: the solute disrupts the orderly packing needed to freeze, so the solution must be cooled further before it solidifies, lowering the freezing point. Both effects scale with the same particle count and van't Hoff factor introduced here, which is exactly what the next two chapters put to work.
